1.title: INTRODUCTION TO ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE & TOGAF
1.text: Welcome to Module 1, where we lay the foundations that every later module builds on. Before we can develop architectures with the ADM, we need to be crystal clear on a few big ideas: what Enterprise Architecture actually is, what TOGAF gives us, and the core vocabulary the exam tests relentlessly. None of this is hard — but it has to be precise. So let's slow down and get the fundamentals genuinely solid.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this module. You'll define Enterprise Architecture, and you'll know exactly what TOGAF means by the word "enterprise" — which is broader than most people expect. You'll be able to explain why organizations invest in EA and the benefits they get. You'll describe what an architecture framework is and what specifically TOGAF provides. You'll name the four architecture domains, BDAT. And you'll get your first proper look at abstraction levels, architecture principles, and building blocks. This module deliberately front-loads the core definitions, because they reappear in almost every exam question.

1.title: What Is Enterprise Architecture?
1.text: Let's start with the headline concept. Enterprise Architecture is the practice of analyzing, designing, planning, and governing an enterprise's structure, so that its business strategy and its technology stay aligned even as everything changes around it. The TOGAF Standard frames the purpose like this: to optimize the often fragmented legacy of processes — both manual and automated — into an integrated environment that's responsive to change and supports the delivery of business strategy. Now here's the single most important thing to internalize: Enterprise Architecture is not just another name for IT architecture. It spans business, data, applications, and technology together. The exam will sometimes plant the statement "EA is just IT architecture" — and that is flatly false. EA is much broader.

1.title: What Is an "Enterprise" in TOGAF?
1.text: Now the word "enterprise," because TOGAF uses it in a very specific way. TOGAF defines an enterprise as any collection of organizations that share a common set of goals. Notice what that does and doesn't say. It could be a whole corporation, or just one division. It could be a government agency or a single department. It could be a chain of organizations linked by common ownership, or a partnership, alliance, consortium, or supply chain. And critically, an enterprise can include partners, suppliers, and customers — not only your internal business units. So the defining feature is common goals, not a single company. An enterprise can stretch right across organizational boundaries, and the exam likes to test exactly that point.

1.title: Why Is an Enterprise Architecture Needed?
1.text: So why do organizations actually need this? The fundamental reason is to manage complexity — specifically, the complexity that appears when a change touches multiple systems with many interdependencies between them. A good Enterprise Architecture helps you strike the right balance between transforming the business and keeping day-to-day operations efficient. It provides a strategic context for how digital capability should evolve as business needs shift. And there's even a compliance angle: much modern privacy legislation demands that processes around personal data are documented clearly enough for untrained readers to follow. If you need one phrase to remember the purpose, it's this — EA optimizes across the enterprise into an integrated environment that's responsive to change.

1.title: Benefits of an Enterprise Architecture
1.text: What do you get in return for the effort? The TOGAF Standard lists a wide range of benefits, and they cluster into five groups. First, better strategic decisions — quicker response to change and stronger support for agility and transformation. Second, more efficient operations — lower costs, capabilities shared across the organization, and a more flexible workforce. Third, more efficient digital delivery — better interoperability, easier upgrades, and improved security. Fourth, better return on investment — reduced complexity and the flexibility to make, buy, or outsource. And fifth, faster and cheaper procurement, because a coherent architectural plan makes buying decisions simpler. Decisions, operations, digital delivery, ROI, and procurement — that's an easy way to hold all five in your head.

1.title: What Prompts an EA Effort?
1.text: What actually triggers an organization to start an EA effort? The standard gives four common drivers. Business-driven initiatives — for example, transforming the business or launching new digital revenue streams. Technology-driven initiatives — like consolidating systems for efficiency and cost reduction. Mergers and acquisitions, where the real return only arrives once technology efficiencies are realized. And managing the technical debt that tends to pile up from fast Agile development. Whatever the specific trigger, the underlying reason is always the same: Enterprise Architecture is there to manage change across many interdependent systems, so that nothing important falls through the cracks.

1.title: What Is an Architecture Framework?
1.text: Let's define the next building-block term: an architecture framework. A framework is a foundational structure — or a set of structures — that you can use to develop a broad range of different architectures. A good one gives you three things: a method for describing both the baseline, or as-is state, and the target, or to-be state; a set of building blocks plus a way to show how they fit together; and a way to plan the evolution from baseline to target. And one more essential point — a framework is meant to be tailored to each organization, establishing a common toolset and a shared vocabulary along the way. So: a reusable structure, plus a method, plus a common language — and always tailored, never used verbatim.

1.title: What the TOGAF Standard Provides
1.text: So what does TOGAF specifically bring to the table? Four pillars. First, a method — the Architecture Development Method, or ADM — a tested, repeatable process for developing architectures. Second, a content framework — a structural model for the work products you produce, so they're consistent. Third, the Enterprise Continuum and Repository — a way to classify and reuse architectural assets instead of reinventing them each time. And fourth, capability and governance guidance — how to actually stand up an architecture practice and govern it properly. Underneath it all, TOGAF is built on an iterative process model, supported by best practices and a reusable set of existing architecture assets. Method, Content, Continuum, Governance — four pillars.

1.title: Two Definitions of "Architecture"
1.text: Here's a subtle point the exam sometimes probes. TOGAF actually uses two complementary definitions of the word "architecture," depending on context. The first comes from the ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 standard: the fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment, plus the principles governing its design and evolution. The second is TOGAF's own working definition: the structure of components, their inter-relationships, and the principles and guidelines governing their design and evolution over time. The nuance to remember is that TOGAF embraces the ISO definition but does not strictly adhere to it — it deliberately keeps its own, more practical wording alongside it. For the exam, just know that two definitions coexist.

1.title: The 4 Architecture Domains (BDAT)
1.text: Now one of the most heavily tested topics in the whole exam — the four architecture domains, which spell BDAT. Business Architecture defines strategy, governance, organization, and key business processes, and it's developed in Phase B. Data Architecture describes the structure of the organization's logical and physical data assets, developed in Phase C. Application Architecture provides the blueprint of applications and how they interact, also in Phase C. And Technology Architecture describes the software and hardware infrastructure capabilities and standards, developed in Phase D. The one thing you absolutely must lock in, shown on screen: Data plus Application together form the Information Systems Architecture, and they're both Phase C. That pairing comes up again and again.

1.title: Other Domains You Can Derive
1.text: The four BDAT domains aren't the end of the story. By combining different views of those core four, an enterprise can define additional, derived domains. Common examples include Information Architecture, Risk and Security Architecture, and Digital Architecture. TOGAF is explicitly designed to enable these multi-dimensional views and to categorize them so an enterprise can consider a wider scope. The exam point is clean and simple: the four core domains are BDAT, and everything else — security, digital, information — is derived by combining views of those four. Don't let a question convince you that security is a fifth core domain.

1.title: The ADM at a Glance
1.text: Let's take a first glance at the ADM — we'll devote all of Module 2 to it, so this is just the orientation. The Architecture Development Method is TOGAF's process for developing architectures. It establishes a framework, develops the architecture content, transitions to it, and governs its realization — all within a continuous, iterative cycle. Here's the crucial exam point: the ADM does not mandate a fixed sequence, and it does not mandate a waterfall method. It's best understood as a reference model of what must be done, not a rigid, one-way process flow. So if a question claims the ADM must always be followed strictly in order, that's false — it's iterative and adaptable.

1.title: Architecture Abstraction Levels
1.text: Architecture work happens at four levels of abstraction, and each one answers a fundamental question. The Contextual level asks "why?" — it's about the environment, the scope, the drivers and goals. The Conceptual level asks "what?" — what's actually needed, usually modeled as services or desired behavior. The Logical level asks "how?" — what kinds of components could organize that functionality, in an implementation-independent way. And the Physical level asks "with what?" — the actual physical components you'll choose to build it. So the progression is why, what, how, with what. One important warning the standard makes explicitly: these are not the Zachman Framework columns. They may sound similar, but TOGAF says there's no connection — don't conflate them.

1.title: Architecture Principles vs Enterprise Principles
1.text: Principles are the next concept. In TOGAF, principles are general rules and guidelines, intended to be enduring and seldom amended, that guide how an organization fulfills its mission. There are two key domains of them. Enterprise Principles provide a basis for decision-making across the entire enterprise — they're the broadest. Architecture Principles relate specifically to architecture work and govern the architecture process itself. And the relationship matters: the hierarchy starts with the Enterprise Principles, and architecture principles — along with any segment-level principles — must live within those boundaries. In other words, Architecture Principles embody and elaborate the broader Enterprise Principles; they can never overstep them. That nesting is the testable idea.

1.title: Architecture Principles — The 4 Components
1.text: TOGAF recommends a standard template for writing a principle, and it has four components — this is a frequently tested fact. The first is the Name, which should capture the essence of the rule and be easy to remember, without naming any specific technology platform. The second is the Statement, which communicates the fundamental rule succinctly and, above all, unambiguously. The third is the Rationale, which highlights the business benefits of following the principle, expressed in business terms. And the fourth is the Implications, which spell out the requirements, costs, and tasks of adopting it — essentially answering the reader's question, "How does this affect me?" So memorize the four: Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications. If a question asks for the components of an architecture principle, that's your answer.

1.title: Architecture Principles — The 5 Qualities
1.text: Beyond the template, TOGAF lists five criteria that distinguish a good set of principles — and the exam likes these too. Understandable: the principle can be quickly grasped by everyone, so violations are minimized. Robust: it's precise enough to support good, enforceable decisions even in controversial situations. Complete: every important principle is defined, covering every situation the enterprise faces. Consistent: principles don't contradict each other, allowing a balanced interpretation. And Stable: principles are enduring, yet an amendment process lets them evolve. Two more facts worth knowing: principles are developed by the enterprise architects with stakeholders and are approved by the Architecture Board, and TOGAF's example set contains twenty-one principles across four groups. So remember the five qualities — Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent, Stable — and that the Architecture Board approves them.

1.title: Deliverables, Artifacts & Building Blocks
1.text: Now three terms that the exam tests constantly, so let's get them precisely right. TOGAF's Content Framework classifies work products in three ways. A deliverable is a contractually specified work product that is formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by stakeholders. An artifact describes a single aspect of the architecture, and takes the form of a catalog, a matrix, or a diagram. And a building block is a potentially reusable component that you combine with other building blocks to deliver solutions. The relationships tie it together: a deliverable contains artifacts, and artifacts are views of building blocks. Keep the one-liners handy — deliverable equals signed off, artifact equals catalog, matrix, or diagram, and building block equals reusable component.

1.title: Artifacts — Catalogs, Matrices, Diagrams
1.text: Let's zoom in on artifacts, because their three classifications are pure exam gold. A catalog is a list of things — for example, a requirements catalog. A matrix shows relationships between things — for example, an application interaction matrix that maps which applications talk to which. And a diagram is a picture of things — for example, a value chain diagram. So the simple memory hook is: catalog equals list, matrix equals relationships, diagram equals picture. If you see a question describing "a list of all applications," that's a catalog. "Which apps connect to which" — that's a matrix. A drawn picture — that's a diagram.

1.title: Architecture vs Solution Building Blocks
1.text: We met ABBs and SBBs in the orientation; let's make the distinction stick. An Architecture Building Block describes a required capability — it's the "what" — and it shapes the specification of the solution building blocks. A Solution Building Block is an actual implementation choice that realizes that capability — it's the "with what." The standard's own example is lovely: "a network" is an Architecture Building Block, an abstract capability; a specific satellite network — say, a swarm of tiny microsatellites versus a few large ones — is a Solution Building Block, a concrete implementation. So remember: ABB is the capability, the what; SBB is the implementation, the with what; and ABBs shape SBBs, not the other way around.

1.title: The Enterprise Continuum (Preview)
1.text: Let's preview the Enterprise Continuum — we'll cover it fully in Module 8. It's a way of classifying the reusable assets in your repository according to how generic or how specific they are. It comprises two complementary continua: the Architecture Continuum, which holds formal architecture descriptions and architecture building blocks, and the Solutions Continuum, which holds implementations and solution building blocks. Assets move along the continuum from the most generic Foundation Architectures, through Common Systems and Industry architectures, all the way to Organization-Specific architectures. The headline to remember is simply: the continuum runs from generic to specific, and it has two halves — Architecture and Solutions.

1.title: The Architecture Repository (Preview)
1.text: Closely related is the Architecture Repository, which we'll also detail in Module 8. Think of it as the place where the outputs of the ADM actually live, stored at different levels of abstraction. It houses eight components — the Architecture Metamodel, the Architecture Capability, the Architecture Landscape, the Standards Library, the Reference Library, the Governance Repository, the Architecture Requirements Repository, and the Solutions Landscape. It's supported by the Enterprise Continuum, which lets stakeholders and practitioners at different levels co-operate. For now, just hold the big idea: the Repository is where your architecture work products are stored and organized.

1.title: Architecture Views & Viewpoints (Preview)
1.text: Two more terms to preview — views and viewpoints — which we'll fully unpack in Module 10. Start from the stakeholder: a stakeholder has concerns. A view is a representation of the architecture from the perspective of a related set of those concerns. A viewpoint defines the conventions for constructing and using a view — so the viewpoint is the template or the specification, and the view is the actual result you produce from it. TOGAF aligns with the ISO 42010 standard on this. The clean way to remember it: the viewpoint is the template or definition, and the view is what you actually see for a specific set of stakeholders. Template versus result.

1.title: Interoperability
1.text: Interoperability is a concept that threads through the whole framework. TOGAF defines it simply as the ability to share information and services. It's commonly categorized three ways: operational or business interoperability, which is how different parts of the enterprise work together; information interoperability, which is how information is shared; and technical interoperability, which is how technical resources connect and are shared. The exam-relevant subtlety is that interoperability is determined progressively throughout the ADM — it's first surfaced in the Architecture Vision, refined through the Business, Data, Application, and Technology phases, and then actually implemented in the Opportunities and Migration phases. It's not handled in a single phase.

1.title: Tailoring TOGAF
1.text: We keep returning to this theme because the exam keeps testing it: TOGAF is a foundational framework, and organizations are expected to customize it during adoption. In practice, that means you deliberately adopt some elements, customize others, exclude some entirely, and create new ones where you need them. The standard even gives an example — you might adopt the TOGAF metamodel but skip all the in-house Technology Architecture guidance because you're a heavy consumer of cloud services. Tailoring applies to the framework itself, to the ADM, and to the deliverables and terminology. So if a question states that TOGAF must be used exactly as written, that's false. Tailoring isn't just allowed — it's expected and encouraged.

1.title: The TOGAF Documentation Set
1.text: A quick word on how the standard is packaged, because the modular structure itself is a concept. The TOGAF Standard, 10th Edition is split into six core documents: Introduction and Core Concepts; the Architecture Development Method; ADM Techniques; Applying the ADM; Architecture Content; and Enterprise Architecture Capability and Governance. Around those sit the TOGAF Library, full of reference material, and the TOGAF Series Guides, with practical how-to guidance. The reason this matters: because the standard is modular, individual parts can evolve independently between editions, rather than everything changing at once. You won't be quizzed on page numbers, but knowing this shape helps everything slot into place.

1.title: TOGAF's Origins
1.text: A little history, because a couple of these facts can show up. TOGAF is developed and maintained by The Open Group Architecture Forum. Version 1, back in 1995, was based on a US Department of Defense framework called TAFIM — the Technical Architecture Framework for Information Management. From that foundation it evolved through many successive versions to reach the 10th Edition in 2022. And throughout, each version has been published openly and may be used freely by any organization developing its own Enterprise Architecture. So the lineage to remember is: TAFIM, then TOGAF version 1 in 1995, evolving all the way to the 10th Edition.

1.title: Key Definitions to Lock In
1.text: Let's consolidate the essential vocabulary on one slide, because these eight terms recur endlessly. An enterprise is a collection of organizations with common goals. An architecture framework is a foundational structure for developing many architectures. An ABB is a required capability — the what. An SBB is an implementation choice — the with what. A deliverable is a contractual, signed-off work product. An artifact is a catalog, matrix, or diagram. A baseline is the starting, as-is architecture. And a target is the desired, to-be architecture. Memorize these one-liners cold — they're the raw material that a large fraction of exam questions are built from. If you know these eight, you'll recognize the right answer fast.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's pre-empt the traps from this module. Trap one: "EA equals IT architecture" — no, EA spans business, data, application, and technology. Trap two: "an enterprise is one company" — no, it's any organizations sharing common goals. Trap three: "the ADM must run as a strict waterfall" — no, it's iterative and tailorable. Trap four: "Data Architecture is Phase B" — no, Data and Application are both Phase C. And trap five: "an ABB is the implementation" — no, the SBB is the implementation; the ABB is the capability. Notice the common thread: almost every trap works by over-narrowing a deliberately broad and flexible framework. When an answer feels too rigid or too small, be suspicious.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Here's your cheat-sheet for this module. Four architecture domains, captured by BDAT. Four abstraction levels — contextual, conceptual, logical, and physical. Two types of building block, ABB and SBB. Three types of content work product — deliverable, artifact, and building block. Three classifications of artifact — catalog, matrix, and diagram. Six core TOGAF documents. Two principle domains — enterprise and architecture. And the origin facts — TOGAF version 1 in 1995, built on TAFIM. Capture this slide; together with the Module 0 cheat-sheet, it covers most of the pure-recall questions you'll face.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's bring it together. Enterprise Architecture aligns business strategy with technology across the whole enterprise — and it is not just IT. An enterprise is any set of organizations with common goals, and an architecture framework is a reusable, tailorable structure for building architectures. TOGAF provides four pillars: a method in the ADM, a content framework, the continuum, and governance. The four domains are BDAT, with Data and Application sharing Phase C. And the core vocabulary you now own includes abstraction levels, principles, building blocks, and the deliverable-versus-artifact distinction. Next, in Module 2, we open up the ADM itself — the heart of the entire framework.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. How does the TOGAF Standard define an "enterprise"? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Any collection of organizations that share a common set of goals In TOGAF an enterprise is any collection of organizations with common goals — it can be a corporation, a division, a government agency, or a partnership/consortium, and may include partners, suppliers, and customers. It is not limited to a single company or to IT.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. Which two architecture domains together form the Information Systems Architecture, and in which ADM phase are they developed? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. Data and Application, in Phase C Data Architecture and Application Architecture together make up the Information Systems Architecture, developed in Phase C. Business is Phase B and Technology is Phase D.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. What is the difference between an Architecture Building Block (ABB) and a Solution Building Block (SBB)? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. An ABB describes a required capability ("what"); an SBB is an implementation choice ("with what") An ABB describes a required capability — the "what" — and shapes the specification of SBBs. A Solution Building Block is an actual implementation choice — the "with what" — that realizes the capability.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. Which set correctly lists the four components of a TOGAF Architecture Principle? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is A. Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications Each architecture principle has four components: Name, Statement, Rationale, and Implications. Option B lists four of the five qualities of a good set of principles (Understandable, Robust, Complete, Consistent, Stable); the other options are domains and architecture states.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. Which statement about tailoring the TOGAF Standard is correct? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is C. Organizations are expected to customize TOGAF — adopting some parts, changing some, excluding some, and creating others TOGAF is a foundational framework that organizations are expected to tailor. They may adopt, customize, exclude, or create elements to fit their context. Treating it as a fixed, unchangeable recipe is the opposite of how TOGAF is intended to be used.
